source.title: Latent Thought Models with Variational Bayes Inference-Time Computation
source.authors: De-Qian Kong; Minglu Zhao; Dehong Xu; Bo Pang; Shu Wang; Edouardo Honig; Zhangzhang Si; Chuan Li; Jian-Wen Xie; Si-Rui Xie; Ying-Nian Wu

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures validation perplexity across scale configurations for a new language-model class, Latent Thought Models, rather than reproducing the original autoregressive scaling-law experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scaling sweeps and arithmetic-reasoning results. Scaling values shown only in figures are recorded as figure-only; cited scaling-law results are not recorded as rows. The paper does not fit or report power-law exponents.
record.test_reason: The paper runs its own scaling sweeps for a new language-model class, Latent Thought Models (LTMs), at 38M–76M parameters. It measures validation perplexity against training tokens and compute, and GSM8K accuracy against model size. It fits no power law, extrapolates nothing and spans only about 2x in parameters. So its bearing on V1 is too weak to read, and its bearing on V6 is only qualitative (r9).
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is largely correct. It should add that the authors find model size has minimal impact at their scale, attributed to embedding compute rivalling attention compute. They present inference steps as the main scaling factor, with latent size as a further axis.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses explicit latent thought vectors, variational Bayes inference, and a dual-rate training process. It evaluates validation perplexity over LTM configurations rather than fitting the original autoregressive scaling-law recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with inference steps and latent size; model-size effects are described as minimal at the tested scale. The paper also notes that scheduling the fast learning rate helps stabilize larger inference-step settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Validation perplexity improves with more variational inference steps (Tfast 16–128) and more latent thought vectors (Nz 24–96). More inference steps improve sample efficiency and, past a compute threshold, compute efficiency.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In latent-variable language models, inference-time optimisation steps and latent size act as additional scaling axes beyond parameters and data.

fits_no_version.finding: An LTM-Large variant with 192 latent vectors gives the best GSM8K performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling latent size improves few-shot reasoning in LTMs.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025; PMLR 267)
record.problems: The scaling curves are presented graphically without fitted exponents or numerical curve values in the text. The tested model-size range is 38M–76M, and the text does not establish power-law behavior over several orders of magnitude. The LTM-Large token count differs between the Introduction and Table 1.
record.rows_left_out: No separately tabulated rows were omitted. The text's qualitative latent-size finding is recorded under fits_no_version because latent size is not named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: Power-law form, exponents, and several orders of magnitude in parameters, tokens or compute.
Quantitative predictability of downstream performance from scale or loss; any fitted relation.
Entire version (the paper calls its compute-optimal guidance preliminary, with no allocation law fitted).
Entire version (depth and width are not varied at fixed parameter count).

missing.what: Validation perplexity across the full configuration sweep (model size × inference steps × latent size). Values are shown only in the figure and no row records them per configuration.

record.verdict_notes: The tested setting is very narrow: about a 2x parameter range at GPT-2 scale on OpenWebText, with no fits or extrapolation. Scaling-law papers are cited as motivation only. LTM perplexities are ELBO upper bounds. Rows r4–r8 are selected-model or baseline comparisons and were unlinked from versions.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not fit power laws or report exponents, test several orders of magnitude, or establish behavior when the other scaling variables are not bottlenecks.
No predictions fitted on small runs are compared with substantially larger runs.
No stable parameter-count and token-count allocation laws are fitted or measured at fixed compute.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The study concerns text language modeling and does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling laws.
The paper reports arithmetic-reasoning results at several model settings, but does not fit a quantitative predictor from pretraining loss or scale to downstream performance.
The study does not compare fitting choices or argue that published exponents disagree or that curves bend away from power laws.

rows.subject: LTM models (model-size sweep)
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size and measured validation perplexity.
rows.note: The authors report that model size has minimal impact at the tested scale, attributing this to embedding-layer computation remaining comparable to attention-layer computation.
rows.check: The authors say model size has minimal impact, but the range is only 38M–76M. Over a 2x range, even Kaplan-type exponents predict a small change, so 'minimal impact' cannot show whether the power law is present or absent. The curves are figure-only and inference steps and latent size are held fixed. Kept as cannot_determine, not partial.

rows.subject: LTM training runs
rows.operation_detail: Varied training-token amount and measured validation perplexity/sample efficiency.
rows.note: The paper describes scaling behavior over training tokens, but gives no fitted functional form or numerical curve values in the text.
rows.check: Figure-only curve with no fitted functional form. It shows perplexity falling with training tokens but cannot establish a power law.

rows.subject: LTM training runs
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation perplexity across training-compute levels and inference-step settings.
rows.note: The text says models with more inference steps become compute-efficient beyond certain compute thresholds; it does not fit a power law.
rows.check: Figure-only compute curves. The text's point is about inference steps becoming compute-efficient beyond a threshold, not power-law form.

rows.subject: LTM-Small
rows.operation_detail: Reported validation perplexity for a representative scaled model.
rows.note: The paper reports this value for a representative model but does not use it to establish a power-law fit.
rows.check: Single selected representative model value, not a scaling measurement. Should not be linked to V1.

rows.subject: LTM-Medium
rows.operation_detail: Reported validation perplexity and compared it with GPT-2-Large at similar training compute.
rows.note: The comparison is about model efficiency, not a power-law fit.
rows.check: Selected model compared with GPT-2-Large: an own-method versus baseline comparison, not a scaling result.

rows.subject: LTM-Large
rows.operation_detail: Reported validation perplexity for a representative model.
rows.note: The Introduction says 3B tokens, while Table 1 lists 0.9B tokens for LTM-Large; the text does not reconcile this discrepancy.
rows.check: Selected model value, and an upper bound. The token count conflicts: 3B in the Introduction, 0.9B in Table 1. Not a scaling measurement.

rows.subject: LTM-Small
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated zero-shot and few-shot arithmetic reasoning on GSM8K using pass@5.
rows.baseline: GPT-2-Medium finetuned on GSM8K and GPT-2-Medium with test-time search, as reported by Li et al. (2022)
rows.value: figure only; text says LTM-Small with 5-shot demonstrations surpasses those baselines
rows.note: The text reports the comparison, but does not provide the numerical pass@5 values.
rows.check: Own method compared with cited GPT-2 baselines from Li et al. (2022). This is not a scale-versus-performance result.

rows.subject: LTM-Small
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated zero-shot arithmetic reasoning on GSM8K using pass@5.
rows.value: figure only; text says LTMs significantly outperform GPT-2 counterparts
rows.note: No numerical result or uncertainty is given in the text.
rows.check: LTM compared with GPT-2 counterparts, a method comparison with no scale dimension. Figure-only.

rows.subject: LTM models (GSM8K size comparison)
rows.operation_detail: Compared arithmetic-reasoning performance across LTM model sizes.
rows.value: figure only; text says increased model size further improves both zero-shot and few-shot performance
rows.note: The figure plots configurations, but the text does not give their individual numerical values.
rows.check: The text says larger LTMs improve zero- and few-shot GSM8K pass@5. The values are figure-only, the sizes span about 2x and no predictive fit is made. The direction matches V6, but the 'predictable' part is not shown.

relationships.condition: LTMs at 38M–76M on GSM8K pass@5, zero- and few-shot
relationships.reason: The text states larger LTMs improve both zero- and few-shot GSM8K (r9). This is qualitative, figure-only and over a narrow size range.
relationships.display_finding: Larger models improved GSM8K pass@5 in both prompting settings across the narrow tested size range.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Model size has minimal impact in this sweep, which the authors attribute to the tested architecture and scale; see r1.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The text reports better arithmetic-reasoning performance with increased model size and reports LTM-Small outperforming the cited baselines in 5-shot evaluation; see r7–r9.
